stem: What does a pulsating abdominal mass indicate?
srcNote: (Vascular) (not so sure about this question but it was very easy and clear)
expl: In an acute presentation, a pulsatile abdominal mass (with pain/shock) points to a ruptured (or symptomatic) AAA.

why.A: Appendicitis gives RIF pain/guarding, not a pulsatile mass.
why.C: A perforated ulcer gives peritonitis, not a pulsatile mass.

stem: Symptom that differs thoracic aortic aneurysm from Abdominal aneurysm?
expl: A thoracic aneurysm compresses intrathoracic structures — the airway (cough, stridor) and the left recurrent laryngeal nerve (hoarseness) — which an abdominal aneurysm cannot do.

srcNote: Abbreviated source recall; the aneurysm type and measurement unit are not stated.
expl: Elective AAA repair is indicated at ≥ 5.5 cm in men (≥ 5.0 cm in women), or with rapid growth or symptoms.

why.C: Above the threshold — repair is already indicated at 5.5.
why.D: 3 cm is the definition of AAA, not a repair threshold.

stem: 54 year old male has undergone CT scan for diverticulitis, the ct scan shows an incidental finding of aortic aneurysm , which of the following is an indication of conservative management ?
expl: A 4-cm asymptomatic AAA is below the repair threshold → conservative management: ultrasound surveillance + risk-factor control (stop smoking, BP, statin).

stem: Which of the following investigations used to diagnose an aortic aneurysm?
expl: Keyed duplex: ultrasound (duplex) is the screening and first diagnostic test for AAA — cheap, no radiation, accurate for diameter. CT angiography is then used for anatomy and operative planning.

why.A: Used for planning (and diagnosis), but the key chose duplex.
why.C: MRI is an alternative, not routine.

stem: what is the most common presentation of abdominal aortic aneurysm?
expl: Most AAAs are asymptomatic and found incidentally on imaging done for something else.

why.B: Rupture is a catastrophic but less common presentation.
why.C: Pain means a symptomatic/expanding AAA — less common.

stem: A 51-year-old man presented for renal stone and a CT was performed, AAA was found, which of the following is an indication for surgery?
expl: Any symptomatic AAA (pain, tenderness) needs urgent repair regardless of size. 3.5–4 cm asymptomatic AAAs are watched; hypertension alone isn't an indication.

stem: What is the most common site of an abdominal aortic aneurysm? (The question text wasn't recalled — only the answer.)
srcNote: only recall. The original source does not supply a complete question or choices.
ansText: Infrarenal abdominal aorta (below the renal arteries) — the most common site of all aneurysms.

stem: A 40 y/o man presented with acute abdominal pain. The triage nurse told you that his oxygen saturation was 97% on air room, pulse 110/min, BP: 80/60 mmHg. When you examined his abdomen there was a pulsatile mass in the epigastrium. Which one of the following is the initial step of management of this patient?
expl: Hypotension + pulsatile epigastric mass = ruptured AAA → immediate laparotomy (permissive hypotension, no CT in an unstable patient).

why.A: Blood is given en route; it isn't the definitive step.

opts.t: Always after surgery of abdominal aortic aneurysm

srcNote: , an aorto-enteric fistula is a connection between the aorta and the intestines, stomach, or esophagus. There can be significant blood loss into the intestines resulting in bloody stool and death. It is usually secondary to an abdominal aortic aneurysm repair. Incomplete source recall; only choice A is supplied.
expl: Aorto-enteric fistula is usually secondary (after AAA graft repair) but primary fistulas from an untreated aneurysm also occur — so "always after AAA surgery" is false. It presents with a herald GI bleed.
